legal.headline: CMRL Exalogic case: ED tells Kerala High Court police bound to register FIR against ex-CM Pinarayi Vijayan
legal.hook: CMRL Exalogic case: ED tells Kerala High Court police bound to register FIR against ex-CM Pinarayi Vijayan
legal.summary: The Enforcement Directorate has argued before the Kerala High Court that police are statutorily bound to register an FIR against former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan in the CMRL Exalogic case. The ED's submission challenges any police reluctance or delay in initiating criminal proceedings. The CMRL Exalogic matter involves allegations that have drawn ED scrutiny under anti-money laundering and possibly corruption statutes. The High Court is now seized of the question whether police have discretion to withhold FIR registration once ED has referred the matter or submitted evidence of cognizable offences. The outcome will clarify the procedural boundary between ED investigations, which operate under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), and police First Information Report registration obligations under the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC). No judgment date has been reported.
legal.contextNote: This hinges on Section 154 CrPC (mandatory FIR registration on receipt of information disclosing cognizable offence) versus police discretion to investigate independently before registration—and ED's role as an information source. (1) For corporates and their counsel tracking ED cases: ED referrals do not automatically compel FIR registration; police retain gate-keeping authority under *Lalita Kumari (2014)*, but ED's evidentiary case may rebut claims of insufficient material. (2) For Pinarayi or co-accused, delayed FIR registration can be challenged via High Court PIL or mandamus under Articles 226/227 Constitution; conversely, premature registration exposes police to abuse of process defences. (3) Watch for whether the Kerala HC distinguishes PMLA investigations (ED's domain, Section 17 PMLA) from CrPC-triggered criminal prosecution—a split ruling could hamper ED enforcement in other states. The precedent will likely affect ongoing ED cases involving public figures.

legal.headline: No Muslim personal law immunity from POCSO case for sex with minor wife: Delhi High Court
legal.hook: No Muslim personal law immunity from POCSO case for sex with minor wife: Delhi High Court
legal.summary: The Delhi High Court has ruled that Muslim personal law does not provide immunity from prosecution under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 for consensual sexual intercourse with a minor wife. The judgment rejects the argument that marriage under personal law—even if valid under Muslim law—can shield a man from criminal liability when the spouse is a child. The court found that POCSO applies irrespective of marital status, as the statute is designed to protect children from sexual abuse without exception. This closes a significant gap in enforcement where defendants previously claimed spousal immunity or personal law protection when charged with sexual offences against minor wives. The ruling aligns statutory child protection with constitutional guarantees and clarifies that no religious or customary law provision overrides POCSO's absolute bar on sexual conduct with minors.
legal.contextNote: This applies POCSO Act §3 (penetrative sexual assault) and §5 (aggravated penetrative sexual assault) as absolute offences with no spousal exemption, overriding any claim under the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 or customary marriage validity. No single landmark precedent had definitively settled this—courts have begun moving in this direction post-*Budharao v. State of Maharashtra* (2021), which broadly construed POCSO, but this is the first explicit High Court rejection of personal law immunity. (1) In-house counsel for NGOs, state prosecutors, and child protection bodies should now treat all POCSO complaints involving minor spouses as falling squarely within statute, without requiring marital law analysis as a defence threshold. (2) M&A and family law practitioners advising clients on personal law disputes or inheritance involving remarriage must flag POCSO exposure if any minor is involved, not treat marriage validity as settling the matter. (3) Watch for possible appeal or clarification on whether this extends to other personal laws (Hindu, Christian) under parallel reasoning.

legal.headline: DTCP can act against building violations in Gurugram municipality: Punjab & Haryana HC in DLF case
legal.hook: DTCP can act against building violations in Gurugram municipality: Punjab & Haryana HC in DLF case
legal.summary: The Punjab & Haryana High Court has ruled that the Department of Town and Country Planning (DTCP) in Haryana retains enforcement authority over building code violations within Gurugram municipality limits, rejecting arguments that municipal boundaries strip the DTCP of jurisdictional powers. The judgment arose from a dispute involving DLF, one of India's largest real estate developers, which had challenged DTCP's action against alleged building violations in its Gurugram projects. The court held that DTCP's statutory mandate under Haryana's town planning legislation remains concurrent and operative even within municipal corporation areas unless explicitly superseded by statute. This clarifies a jurisdictional grey zone that had permitted developers to exploit conflicting claims of authority between municipal bodies and the state planning regulator. The ruling potentially exposes ongoing or completed DLF projects in Gurugram to renewed scrutiny and remediation orders from DTCP.
legal.contextNote: The judgment interprets the Haryana Development and Regulation of Urban Areas Act (HDRUA) and related town planning rules. The high court has rejected the 'municipal boundary exclusion' doctrine that some developers had invoked to evade DTCP oversight. (1) Real estate counsel advising on Gurugram/NCR projects must now assume dual regulatory exposure: municipal corporation *and* DTCP concurrently hold enforcement power over building code compliance, zoning, and structural violations—developers cannot rely on municipal incorporation as a shield. (2) Remediation timelines and cost allocations in ongoing DLF disputes should be reassessed; DTCP recovery notices or demolition orders may now survive appeal if the regulator acts within this reaffirmed mandate. (3) Due diligence on completed Gurugram residential/commercial projects should examine DTCP compliance certificates and correspondence separately from municipal approvals, as the two are not fungible.
